articles.title: BAE Systems to Offer Bofors Tridon Mk2 to Indian Army
articles.text:
BAE Systems are looking to partner with an Indian Industry partner to produce its Bofors Tridon Mk2 mobile air defence system. The 40mm system, which originates from Sweden is being geared up to meet increasing demand from India for air defence systems to protect its forces and key assets against new threats such as drones, loitering munitions etc.
This comes after production started on the BvS10 Sindhu at Larsen & Toubro’s Armoured Systems Complex in Gujarat. The production partnership was signed between BAE Systems and L&T in 2025. The Indian Army have ordered an initial 18 units.
Tony Walton, Managing Director BAE Systems India said they are looking at producing Tridon Mk2 with an Indian partner. They want to support India’s focus on domestic production.
The Bofors Tridon Mk2 is a mobile remote-controlled air defence system based around a 40mm anti-aircraft gun. It uses proven Bofors guns combined with modern fire control systems and smart ammunition.
It is capable of engaging a wide variety of threats such as UAS, loitering munitions, helicopters, fixed-wing aircraft and cruise missiles. The system can be used as part of an AAD network or independently using the sensor and fire control suite.
One main feature of the system is it’s compatibility with Bofors 3P smart ammunition. The ammunition can be programmed to be used in various situations. This includes proximity fuses for engaging aerial targets. This is particularly useful when engaging against drones due to the challenge of engaging such a small highly manoeuvrable target with traditional ammunition.
A gun-based solution can also be used as an alternative to expensively launching guided missiles against cheap drones. However this depends on a number of factors such as threat detection, engagement range, ammunition usage and integration with other AAD systems. The Indian Army are improving their ability to counter the increasingly diverse aerial threats. Small drones can be used for reconnaissance, directing artillery fire and attacking exposed vehicles/forward positions. Larger drones and loitering munitions can also pose a threat to logistic centres, command posts and other military assets.
A mobile 40mm system could be used to provide an extra layer of protection against these threats. This could be done in situations where launching a missile would be unnecessary or un-economic. The mobility of the gun means it could be used to travel with ground formations or provide cover for certain areas.
India do have gun-based AAD solutions currently available such as the Sudarshan CIWS produced by L&T. This means Tridon Mk2 could be introduced in a market where the domestic solution would need to be analysed. An Indian production solution would give BAE Systems access to a large market and support India’s localisation goals. They already have a partnership with L&T from the BvS10 Sindhu so could start discussions with them however there is no confirmation that L&T will be chosen to produce Tridon Mk2.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

articles.title: GTRE Eyes Private Sector for Kaveri 2.0 Engine Development
articles.text:
Encouraged by results after awarding a contract to a private sector company to make modules for the Kaveri derivative engine (KDE) for the first time in the country, GTRE is now planning to rope in one or two Private sector companies as major partners in the development of a new Core for the proposed Kaveri 2.0 engine, in case the program is granted the go-ahead and gets funds for its development by the Defence Ministry.
Officials from the organisation told idrw. that private sector help will allow them to compress some parts of the proposed schedule that could have been required to make a new core that could generate 55kN above of Dry Thrust. GTRE is a research-and-design establishment, not a volume manufacturer, and the DcPP model explicitly assigns the industrialisation burden to a private partner, but getting them as a partner will allow their talent to be used to solve complex issues with the new core and later use them to co-develop tooling’s , inspection systems and subsystem testing for the new engine.
Godrej Aerospace is manufacturing the dry variant of the GTRE GTX-35VS Kaveri engine for the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) to power India’s stealth drones and unmanned platforms, and GTRE is already showing confidence in the DcPP and soon will allow them to carry out most of the testing that was earlier carried out by them after deliveries of each engine module.
idrw has been told that private firms have demonstrated that they can develop component level deveopment task can be outsourced to them, and getting them as major partners in the program will also reduce the load on GTRE, thus also ensuring that the engine doesn’t take 30 years to mature like seen in the current Kaveri engine program.
One or two major partners in the program, supported by a dozen local suppliers in the supply chain, can fast-track the program to develop a new 90kN engine as a replacement for the F-404 engines that, in the next 15-20 years, will need to be replaced. Current engine production has highlighted that, while GE is showing plans to increase its production of the same engine to meet local and export demands after the engine was selected to power both T-7 and Hurjet jets, indicating that the engine will remain in production for more 15 years atleast, but it is not confirmation that the supply chain won’t be affected.
GTRE will also be co-developing a new engine for the AMCA Program and will be getting the latest access to the technology to develop a 5th gen engine for the program, and it becomes crucial that further development of the new Kaveri engine also incorporates some of the technologies that will be developed for the program so that the new engine is vastly superior to the F-404 that it plans to replace.

articles.title: A Nuclear Strike On Iran? It Sounds Absurd Because It Is. Let’s Talk About It
articles.text:
On Sunday evening, commentator Tucker Carlson made a chilling claim: U.S. President Donald Trump may soon use nuclear weapons against Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain facility. Carlson’s comments were posted on X just two days ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, which Trump has frequently used as a timeframe for when he would conduct a new wave of airstrikes on Iran if he so decides. However, earlier on Monday, Trump downplayed that deadline, answering “no” when asked by reporters whether he was considering attacking after the election is over.

Regardless, Carlson’s claim runs counter to the president’s previous stance on the nuclear weapons issue. Trump has publicly eschewed their use, and while he has discussed attacking Pickaxe Mountain, he’s made it clear it would be by a conventional weapon if he made the call.

Monday afternoon, the White House dismissed Carlson’s asssertion.

“President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe,” a White House official told us. “Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief’s thinking.”

We don’t know the source of Carlson’s information or if it is in any way accurate. Carlson has experienced a major rift with Trump and has said plenty of shocking things in recent years, especially in regard to Trump’s second term and the war with Iran. Still, he is a very connected figure in right-wing media. Regardless, as TWZ editor-in-chief Tyler Rogoway noted on X, even conjecture that has gone viral about the potential use of a nuclear weapon for the first time since the U.S. bombed Nagasaki on Aug. 9, 1945, merits discussion. It would have such profound and irrevocable repercussions that it should not be ignored. We addressed the same concerns in regard to Russia and Ukraine in 2022.

“If a nuclear weapon were used on [Pickaxe Mountain] in Iran by the US or Israel or an empty field in Ukraine by Russia etc, it doesn’t matter, it would open up Pandora’s box and would make the U.S. and the world dramatically less safe,” Rogoway stated. “This isn’t even a question of how big of a disaster the use, in any manner, of a nuclear weapon would be. It would represent the largest foreign policy error ever by the United States if we were involved. We can only hope this claim isn’t accurate in any way.”

“…And I have no idea if this claim has merit, but this is important nonetheless,” he added in his X thread. “It is massively viral on my X feed. It has to be addressed.”

Pickaxe Mountain, a very hardened Iranian facility also known as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, is located in central Iran. As we have noted previously, it is deeply buried and would be a very difficult target to effectively destroy. In the past, Iran has openly discussed plans to produce centrifuges to support its nuclear enrichment efforts at the newer facility located there. It is also estimated to be large enough to house an actual enrichment plant, as well as other nuclear infrastructure, but exactly what is inside remains unconfirmed. Our previous reporting provides deeper insights into Pickaxe Mountain and Iran’s possible intentions for it.

What Carlson said

“Under pressure from Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran,” Carlson stated on X. “The target would be Pickax Mountain in central Iran, where Israeli intelligence claims the Iranian government has restarted its nuclear enrichment program. No conventional weapon in the American arsenal can penetrate 300 feet of solid granite to destroy the tunnels where enrichment is supposedly taking place.”

“The only military option is a nuclear strike. Netanyahu has been pushing hard for one,” the commentator added. “‘Bibi calls Trump about it every day,’ says an informed observer. Netanyahu is cornered and desperate. After last week’s election results, he can’t form a government unless Trump intervenes directly in Israeli politics and brokers a deal with other parties that gives Netanyahu 61 seats in the Knesset. Otherwise, he is out as prime minister and on his way to ignominy, investigations and possibly jail. Netanyahu must stay close to Trump. He needs this war.”

What Trump has said about using nuclear weapons

“We don’t need it. Why do I need it?” Trump responded in April when asked if he would use nuclear weapons against Iran. “Why would a stupid question like that be asked? Why would I use a nuclear weapon where we’ve totally in a very conventional way decimated them without it.” 

“A nuclear weapon should never be allowed to be used by anybody,” he added.

The American leader reiterated that stance in August.

“They’re totally defeated militarily, so I defeat them, and now I should use a nuclear weapon on top of them? What a stupid question,” Trump responded on Aug. 31 when again asked by a reporter if he would use nuclear weapons against Iran.

Still, Trump sparked concerns about whether he would use nuclear weapons when he threatened to obliterate Iran in April in a social media post.

“A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again,” Trump stated on his Truth Social site. “I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will.”

Several experts we spoke with downplayed the chances that Trump would order a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain, but they did not completely rule it out.

“Is it likely? No,” Daryl G. Kimball, Executive Director of the Arms Control Association (ACA) and publisher and contributor for the organization’s monthly journal, Arms Control Today, said when we asked if he thought Trump would order a nuclear strike. “Is it possible that an unstable desperate president who has sole authority to authorize nuclear weapons use, would do so, yes. Given the situation, it is crucial that responsible U.S. voices and international leaders speak out against a massive U.S. strike on Iran of any kind.”

“That is highly unlikely,” Hans Kristensen — director, Nuclear Information Project, Federation of American Scientists, explained to us. He also writes the bi-monthly Nuclear Notebook and the world nuclear forces overview in the SIPRI Yearbook. “There is nothing at all in Iran that justifies breaking the 81-year absence of nuclear weapons use. It would be a violation of the international Laws of War, have devastating consequences for U.S. foreign policy and the efforts to prevent proliferation and the use of nuclear weapons. It would be the kind of act where one would hope the people in the nuclear chain of command would refuse to carry out the president’s order.”

“I honestly don’t know that anyone knows that Trump will or won’t do, including Trump,” Stephen I. Schwartz, nonresident senior fellow at the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, told us. “… for many years, often without prompting, he has spoken with a mix of wariness and awe about the tremendous power of nuclear weapons. But he has also publicly and repeatedly threatened to utterly annihilate North Korea, Afghanistan, and Iran. So, really, who knows?”

What weapon could the U.S. use if Trump ordered a nuclear strike?

As we have reported in the past, the B61-11 is the only air-delivered nuclear weapon in the U.S. stockpile today that is specifically designed to address this target set. 

“The B61-11 is based on the earlier B61-7, but is substantially different in form and function. It has a heavily reinforced outer shell, possibly with a depleted uranium penetrating nose section, and a rocket booster at the rear to help it penetrate down into underground facilities. Sources differ on the maximum yield of the B61-11, but it is said to either be between 340 and 360 kilotons (identical to that of the B61-7) or to be closer to 400 kilotons. There are also reportedly fewer than 100 of these bombs in the stockpile.”

The first B61-11 versions entered service in the 1960s. We have written extensively about the entire family of these weapons.

Given the yield of the B61-11, “one could probably do the job” of rendering Pickaxe Mountain unusable, Kristensen told us. “The collateral damage from 400 kilotons would be considerable; even if some very deep structures potentially survived, the damage to the overall infrastructure — plus the residual radiation in the soil — would probably make the site unusable. Other potential options include more conventional penetrator attacks to take out access points and accessible infrastructure, or potentially cyber attacks to sabotage or disable equipment and functions.”

“I think there are many non-nuclear options the United States and/or Israel could utilize to prevent Iran from restarting its nuclear weapons program (if, indeed, Iran has made a decision to do that),” argued Schwartz. “That would include using guided conventional bombs to target any entrances to the facility, impeding efforts of personnel to gain access and also complicating/preventing the movement of any materials out of the mountain.”

“Using an ICBM [intercontinental ballistic missile] would not be a good option,” he added. “For one thing, any ICBM would have to fly over Russia to reach Iran, which would be risky in more ways than one, even if Putin somehow agreed to allow that to happen. For another, ICBM warheads are not designed to penetrate the earth, at least not to any significant depth, so the force of the explosion would largely be ‘wasted’ on the surface, with everything that implies about lethal radioactive fallout. (Using an SLBM [submarine-launched ballistic missile] from a Trident submarine stationed closer to Iran would avoid the overflight risks but would also still be perceived as a threat by Russia and perhaps China after launch, even if we notify them in advance. But W76 and W76-1 warheads are not earth-penetrators, and I doubt we would want to use a 455-kiloton W88, our largest ballistic missile warhead, also not a deep earth-penetrator.)”

Israel has a nuclear weapons program that it does not publicly acknowledge and can deliver warheads via its Jericho ballistic missiles, some tactical jets and maybe even submarines.

It’s possible a special operations forces teams could attempt to raid the facility, access its interior and place a nuclear device inside it, although such a mission would be immensely challenging and extremely risky. We have also talked about the possibility of irradiating the facilities from the inside without using a nuclear warhead, but instead planting and detonating a kind of dirty bomb.

What are the alternatives to nuclear weapons?

As we noted earlier in this story, Trump has brought up the issue of conventional weapons to attack Pickaxe Mountain. In July, he said it was ripe for a “nice big fat shot right in the front door.”

At the time, we discussed how difficult it would be to effectively destroy or render inoperable a hardened, deeply buried facility like Pickaxe.

For years, experts have talked about the likelihood that the main caverns under the mountain are beyond the reach of even the largest known conventional bunker buster bomb in U.S. inventory, the 30,000-pound-class GBU-57/B Massive Ordnance Penetrator (MOP). The MOP was developed, at least in part, specifically to hold underground facilities in Iran at risk. Construction at Pickaxe Mountain, especially in the past five years, is a clear response to U.S. threats.

MOPs were the centerpiece during the June 2025 Operation Midnight Hammer strikes, with 12 being dropped on Fordow and another two on Natanz. To get at the actual targets at Fordow, six MOPs were dropped on two specific ventilation shafts, with each successive bomb burrowing deeper down into the complex below. This underscores the challenges that would be involved in attempting a similar operation against Pickaxe Mountain. It is unclear how many MOPs the U.S. has left or whether there are enough to have the same kind of effects on Pickaxe Mountain as they had on Fordow and Natanz. We also don’t even know if any features of the installation, like the ventilation shafts, even exist there to be exploited.

CBS News reported last month that the White House and Pentagon “have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb [MOAB] to hit military sites in Iran,” including Pickaxe Mountain, “if ordered by President Trump.” However, the 22,000-pound-class MOAB, also designated the GBU-43/B, is not a deep-penetrating munition, it’s a fuel-air bomb, and it was not immediately clear from that story how the weapon might be employed. The bomb is also only known to be currently cleared for employment via C-130-type aircraft. It has only been used in combat once, in Afghanistan in 2017, where the skies above were entirely permissive. 

MOAB’s use case would be limited against sites like Pickaxe Mountain. While its unique overpressure effects could harm any personnel exposed inside tunnel systems that are open to the outside world, it is unlikely to destroy or even heavily damage the hardened facilities themselves. It could cause damage to external support infrastructure and act as a psychological weapon in its own right, but it is not a bunker buster in any way.

As mentioned earlier, although for a nuclear weapon insertion mission, a much more dangerous option for American forces would be sending U.S. troops directly into Iran to secure and destroy the facility.

“Special Operations Forces [SOF] could render the site off-limits, at least for a time, but that would be a much riskier operation,” Schwartz noted. 

We addressed the SOF option earlier this year in an interview with former U.S. Central Command commander Joseph Votel, who discussed the enormous challenges of putting boots on the ground so deep into Iranian territory. We have frequently discussed the complexities, and pros and cons of a commando raid on an underground nuclear facility.

In a 2024 raid on a Syrian underground missile site, Israeli special operations forces used explosives they brought with them in order to blow up the underground facility, including sophisticated machinery, from inside.

Still doing this deep in Iran could require a relatively large force and an operation that could last days and would include occupying and defending a key area within the country as teams try to access the caverns. It depends on just how accessible and defended Pickaxe Mountain is.

The fallout dangers of using a nuclear weapon against Iran

The B61-11 “would dig up and disperse into the atmosphere large amounts of radioactive material,” Kristensen told us. 

He pointed to the results he derived from the NUKEMAP nuclear weapons explosion effects simulation site to offer a sense of what could happen.

“A surface burst would, depending on wind conditions, spread debris nearly 300 km downwind,” he explained. “Perhaps further, because the simulation calculates a surface bust, while the B61-11 would penetrate a few meters into the rock and therefore increase the fallout issue.”

If highly enriched uranium was stored underground, it would be hard to determine what would happen to it in such an attack, Kristensen added.

“It depends on how the attack is carried out,” Kristensen noted. “It could potentially be entombed or some of it could be lifted up into the atmosphere.”

“U.S. politicians and some civilian military leaders have, since the first Gulf War, periodically and misleadingly claimed that earth-penetrating nuclear weapons can safely and reliably destroy deeply-buried and hardened underground targets with no significant consequences above ground,” Schwartz proffered. “Nothing could be further from the truth, for the simple reason that earth-penetrating nuclear weapons have to, you know, penetrate the earth. That leaves a hole out of which radioactive dirt and gases will spew following any nuclear explosion (as happened more than once at the Nevada Test Site during the Cold War, when nuclear test shafts thought to be properly and fully stemmed or sealed failed, releasing vast and dangerous amounts of radioactive debris, contaminating both the test site and areas downwind.”)

“The larger the explosion, the larger the venting,” Schwartz added. “Depending on which way the winds are blowing, downwind of Pickaxe Mountain could include Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Russia, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan.”

What about the geopolitical fallout?

In his X post, Carlson offered a blunt assessment of the geopolitical ramifications of a U.S. nuclear strike on Iran.

“An American nuclear attack on Iran would set a new precedent,” he stated. “The Russians have already told at least two other governments that an American nuclear strike on Iran would free them to use nuclear weapons against Ukraine. Pakistan and India would be tempted to do the same against each other, as would North Korea against Seoul. After the first nuclear strike, World War Three is inevitable.”

As we have frequently reported, Putin has rattled the nuclear saber against the West as well as in Ukraine since the early days of his full-on invasion of that country.

“The United States has, Republican and Democratic administrations alike, worked hard to ensure that the achievement of no nuclear weapons use since 1945 is continued,” Kristensen told us. “If the Trump regime were to break that taboo, especially in a situation where there is no imminent or executed Iranian nuclear threat to the United States or its allies, it would turn the United States into the nuclear pariah. It would threaten political relations with allies that have also worked to prevent the use of nuclear weapons. And, yes, if the United States were to break the taboo, other nuclear armed states would feel less inhibited — Putin included.”

“If Trump decides to attack Iran with nuclear weapons in a purely preventive war of choice (with Iran presenting no imminent or probably even short-term threat, making such an attack illegal under international law), it will almost certainly unleash both global condemnation (apart from Israel) and a new wave of nuclear proliferation that will be extremely difficult if not impossible to stop,” said Schwartz. “That would be highly counterproductive for the United States and its allies. And while I am not an economist, it’s not hard to imagine there will be severe and negative global economic repercussions as well.”

The sentiments expressed by the nuclear experts echo what Rogoway stated on X.

“The potential game trees for many potential hotspots around the globe post use would be so terrifying it’s hard to comprehend,” he wrote. “All the softer levers the U.S. once had to deter such a thing, which has been effective for the better part of a century would vanish. Proliferation would explode. The U.S. would likely no longer be a superpower beyond it’s military capabilities and likely short-term wealth. [Every] ounce of moral highground would evaporate. The entire world would be on the brink by default.”

He also stated that this would quickly destroy key alliances.

We have no direct information about whether Trump is even contemplating the use a nuclear weapons against Iran or not. However, a discussion of the wide-ranging ramifications of such an unprecedented act is a worthwhile exercise, especially in these uncertain times, and even more so if this possibility has actually been floated within the administration.

articles.title: Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B
articles.text:
Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion.

The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads.

Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms.

Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt.

However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure.

Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so.

Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion.

Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions.

Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion.

Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU.

The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments.

The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution. The likes of Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are some of the model dev's biggest compute providers, but according to the filing, cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44 percent of its revenue in the nine months ended September 30.

Anthropic insists that none of its customers account for more than 10 percent of revenue. Yet reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they are all either actively developing competing products or provide access to models from Anthropic's rivals.

Despite all the risks in its prospectus, Anthropic believes it can become a sustainable business if it can access enough compute capacity. And by doing so, the prospectus claims AI will reshape the economy "in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet."

With so much at stake, how can humanity afford not to spend like a drunken sailor? ®

articles.title: Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware
articles.text:
Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot.

Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating.

Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.”

One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said.

Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer.

The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote.

While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted.

Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher.

One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote.

The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.

While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

articles.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
articles.text:
It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light.

Why large dogs age faster

In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science.

The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off)  across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.

articles.title: These smart glasses promise to turn your silent mouth movements into text
articles.text:
The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound.

Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable.

Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be.

As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text.

“We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.”

This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you.

“The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said.

In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital.

Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed.

“Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.”

They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns.

“We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.”

With just four months of work under their belts, Subvocal could be a massive hit, ushering in a new era of silent muttering productivity for workers in a variety of industries, or it could flop as it tries to scale.

Those interested in finding out can preorder a pair now for $199, with the other $300 not due until the glasses ship. ®

A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday. The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized. In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy.

"Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. articles.title: AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes
articles.text:
If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos.

Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale.

"Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation."

Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps.

To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as "Legal Zero-Days: A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and "Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System" [PDF].

The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace. Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well."

Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code.

The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications.

Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world.

To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm.

For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid.

Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made.

"We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves."

Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly.

"Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts. Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases.

"This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process."

Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit.

"I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified."

Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term.

"Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®
